Today we find out how fast
a wave travels, and why.
Part 1: What a wave is.

A wave carries energy
from one place to another.

The medium itself only moves back
and forth around where it was.

Sound in air and light from
the sun are both waves.

Drop a stone in a pond
and ripples spread out.

The water stays where it is;
the energy moves outwards.

Many people think a louder
sound travels faster.

It does not: loudness changes the
amplitude, and the speed stays the same.

Watch the pulse travel along the
slinky while each coil stays put.
Part 2: Wave speed.

The wavelength is the distance
between two neighbouring crests.

We write it with the Greek letter
lambda and measure it in metres.

Frequency is how many waves
pass a point each second.

The period is the time
one wave takes to pass.

Amplitude is how far the
medium moves from rest.

Wave speed equals
frequency times wavelength.

Speed in metres per second, frequency
in hertz, wavelength in metres.

Double the frequency at the same
speed and the wavelength halves.

Before we go on: what happens to the
wavelength if the frequency doubles?

Hold on to your guess. We
will check it in a moment.

Let us try a note of four
hundred and forty hertz in air.

We know the frequency and the speed of
sound, three hundred and forty three.

Rearrange the equation so the
wavelength is speed over frequency.

Divide, and the wavelength comes out
at about seventy eight centimetres.

Sound moves at about three hundred
and forty metres per second in air.

In water it is four times faster,
and in steel faster still.
